name: Device Management Access
author: Recurse
subject: networking
description: Choose between console, Telnet, SSH, HTTP, HTTPS, TACACS+, RADIUS and cloud management, and set up secure SSH-only access.

lesson.intro: Every router, switch and controller needs a way for you to log in and manage it. The CCNA blueprint lists the options: console, Telnet, SSH, HTTP, HTTPS, AAA with TACACS+ or RADIUS, and cloud management. This lesson explains how each one works, when you would use it and which ones are safe, and it previews the SSH-only configuration you will build for real in the SSH lab later in the path.
objectives: Distinguish out-of-band console, AUX and management-port access from in-band Telnet, SSH, HTTP and HTTPS access
Configure line authentication (line passwords, login local, enable secret) and SSH-only vty access, and verify it
Explain why SSH and HTTPS replace Telnet and HTTP, including their port numbers
Compare TACACS+ and RADIUS and configure AAA logins with a local fallback
Describe how cloud-managed devices such as Cisco Meraki are provisioned and managed

sections.title: Out-of-band: the console port
sections.body:
You unbox a new switch. It has no IP address, so nothing on the network can reach it. The only way in is the **console port**: a serial connection from your laptop, using a rollover (console) cable to the RJ-45 console port, or a USB cable to the USB console port that many newer devices have. A terminal emulator such as PuTTY connects with the defaults: **9600 bits per second, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit, no flow control**.

The console is **out-of-band** management: it does not depend on the production network. That makes it essential for initial setup, password recovery and fixing a device after a bad change has cut off its network access. Larger networks extend the idea with a **terminal server** (console server) cabled to the console ports of many devices, often on a separate management network, so engineers can reach every console remotely even during an outage. Older routers also have an **AUX** port, an asynchronous serial port meant for a dial-in modem, which gives the same out-of-band reach over a phone line. And many current routers, switches and controllers have a dedicated **management Ethernet port** (for example GigabitEthernet0 on many routers or Gi0/0 on Catalyst 9000 switches) kept in its own management routing table, so it can sit on an out-of-band management network that never carries user traffic.

Anything you reach through the normal network, using an IP address on an SVI or a routed interface, is **in-band** management: Telnet, SSH, HTTP, HTTPS, SNMP and so on. It is convenient, but it fails when the network fails.

Even the console needs protection, because anyone with physical access can plug in, and by default a new device lets anyone at the console straight in. The simplest sound setup uses a local username and an idle timeout, covered in the next section.
sections.code:
Out-of-band (works when the production network is down)
  Laptop ---- console cable (RJ-45 or USB) ----> SW1 console port
  Engineer -> terminal server -----------------> console ports of many devices
  Mgmt network ------------------------------> dedicated management Ethernet port
  Modem (older routers) ---------------------> AUX port

In-band (rides the production network)
  Admin PC -- SSH / HTTPS / SNMP across the LAN --> SW1 SVI 10.1.99.11
sections.pitfall: Assuming the console is safe because it is physical. Wiring closets get opened, and a console session left logged in is an open door. Use login local and an exec-timeout.

check.question: A bad change removed a switch's only management IP address, cutting off all remote access. How can an engineer still reach the CLI?
choices: Through SSH on TCP 22, which does not need an IP address
Through the console port, which is out-of-band
Through HTTPS on TCP 443
Through Telnet from the default gateway
check.explanation: The console is a direct serial connection that does not depend on IP or the production network. SSH, HTTPS and Telnet are all in-band and need a reachable IP address.

sections.title: Line passwords, local usernames and enable secret
sections.body:
Every way into the CLI lands on a **line**: line console 0 for the console, line aux 0 for the AUX port and line vty 0 15 (or 0 4) for Telnet and SSH sessions. Each line decides how users authenticate, and the choices are worth knowing exactly, because exam exhibits show them.

- **`password` plus `login`**: a shared line password with no username. Everyone types the same password. Simple, anonymous, and not accepted by SSH, which always needs a username.
- **`login local`**: the line checks the local username database built with `username admin secret ...`. Each person has an account, and log messages record who made changes.
- **AAA**: after `aaa new-model`, method lists (next sections) decide, usually pointing at a TACACS+ or RADIUS server with local as the fallback.
- **No login at all**: the factory default on the console, so anyone with a cable gets user EXEC mode. Vty lines default to `login` with no password set, which refuses every Telnet session with 'Password required, but none set'.

Once logged in, users are in user EXEC mode (the > prompt). The `enable` command moves them to privileged EXEC (#) and asks for the **enable password**. Configure it with `enable secret`, which stores a strong hash; the older `enable password` is stored in clear text (or weakly scrambled by `service password-encryption`) and is ignored when an enable secret exists. Local accounts should likewise use `username NAME secret` rather than `username NAME password`.

Finish every line with `exec-timeout` (minutes and seconds) so an abandoned session closes itself, and `logging synchronous` on the console so log messages do not break up what you type.
sections.code:
SW1(config)# enable secret Str0ngEnable
SW1(config)# username admin secret Str0ngPa55
SW1(config)# line console 0
SW1(config-line)# login local
SW1(config-line)# exec-timeout 5 0
SW1(config-line)# logging synchronous
SW1(config-line)# line vty 0 15
SW1(config-line)# login local
SW1(config-line)# exec-timeout 10 0

! A vty line with plain login but no password refuses everyone:
PC> telnet 10.1.99.11
Password required, but none set
[Connection to 10.1.99.11 closed by foreign host]
sections.pitfall: Configuring a line password and login local together and expecting the password to work. login local ignores the line password; users need a username and its secret.

check.question: Line console 0 has both password Cisco123 and login local, and username admin secret Str0ng exists. What does a user at the console have to enter?
choices: Only the line password Cisco123
The username admin and its password Str0ng
Nothing, because the console is never protected
The enable secret only
check.explanation: login local tells the line to use the local username database, so the line password is ignored. A shared line password would be used only with the plain login command.

sections.title: In-band access: giving a switch an IP address
sections.body:
To manage a Layer 2 switch remotely, it needs an IP address, but its physical ports are switchports with no IP. The address goes on a **switch virtual interface (SVI)**, a logical interface in a VLAN: interface vlan 1 by default, or better, a dedicated management VLAN. A Layer 2 switch also needs `ip default-gateway` so it can reply to administrators in other subnets; it does not route, so this is how it reaches anything off its own subnet. A switch can also learn its management address with `ip address dhcp` on the SVI, which is handy for zero-touch setups. A router or Layer 3 switch simply uses one of its routed interfaces, an SVI or a loopback (a loopback never goes down while any path to the router exists, so it makes a stable management address).

Once it has an address, the device accepts remote logins on its **vty lines** (virtual terminal lines). Each Telnet or SSH session uses one vty line. Switches typically have 16 (line vty 0 15); many routers have 5 (line vty 0 4) by default, though it varies by platform. Under line vty, `login local` checks the local username database, and `transport input` decides which protocols may connect.

The example puts the management address in VLAN 99. The SVI comes up only when VLAN 99 exists and at least one port in it is up and forwarding, usually the uplink trunk, so VLAN 99 must also be allowed on that trunk.
sections.code:
SW1(config)# vlan 99
SW1(config-vlan)# name MGMT
SW1(config-vlan)# interface vlan 99
SW1(config-if)# ip address 10.1.99.11 255.255.255.0
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# exit
SW1(config)# ip default-gateway 10.1.99.1
sections.pitfall: Forgetting ip default-gateway on a Layer 2 switch. Admins in the same subnet can connect, but everyone else gets no reply, because the switch has no way to send traffic off its subnet.

check.question: A Layer 2 switch has 10.1.99.11/24 on interface vlan 99. Admins in 10.1.99.0/24 can SSH to it, but admins in 10.2.0.0/16 cannot. Which command is most likely missing?
choices: ip routing
transport input all
ip default-gateway 10.1.99.1
no shutdown under interface vlan 1
check.explanation: Without a default gateway, the switch cannot reply to hosts outside its own subnet. ip routing would turn a Layer 3 switch into a router, which is not what a Layer 2 switch needs here.

sections.title: Telnet versus SSH, and the SSH-only setup
sections.body:
**Telnet** (TCP port 23) gives you a remote CLI, but everything, including the username and password, crosses the network in clear text. Anyone capturing packets on the path reads your credentials. It has no place on a production network.

**SSH** (Secure Shell, TCP port 22) gives the same CLI over an encrypted, authenticated session. Use **SSH version 2**; version 1 has known weaknesses. To run SSH, IOS needs an RSA key pair. To generate the keys it needs a hostname and a domain name, because it names the key after the device's fully qualified domain name (for example SW1.example.com). SSH also needs username-based login, so it pairs with login local or AAA.

Here is the standard SSH-only setup. You will configure it in the SSH lab later in the path; for now, read it line by line:

- `hostname` and `ip domain-name`: build the FQDN that names the key.
- `crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048`: create the key pair (SSH version 2 needs at least 768 bits; use 2048).
- `ip ssh version 2`: refuse version 1 clients.
- `username admin secret ...`: a local account with the password stored as a hash.
- `line vty 0 15` and `login local`: check usernames on all 16 vty lines.
- `transport input ssh`: allow only SSH, so Telnet is refused.
- `exec-timeout 10 0`: close idle sessions after 10 minutes.

The next section shows how to verify it and use it.
sections.code:
SW1(config)# hostname SW1
SW1(config)# ip domain-name example.com
SW1(config)# crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048
The name for the keys will be: SW1.example.com
% The key modulus size is 2048 bits
% Generating 2048 bit RSA keys, keys will be non-exportable...
[OK] (elapsed time was 3 seconds)
SW1(config)# ip ssh version 2
SW1(config)# username admin secret Str0ngPa55
SW1(config)# line vty 0 15
SW1(config-line)# login local
SW1(config-line)# transport input ssh
SW1(config-line)# exec-timeout 10 0
SW1(config-line)# end
SW1# show ip ssh
SSH Enabled - version 2.0
Authentication timeout: 120 secs; Authentication retries: 3
! lines omitted
sections.pitfall: Setting transport input ssh on line vty 0 4 only. On a switch with 16 lines, lines 5 to 15 still accept Telnet. Apply the SSH-only settings to every vty line the device has.

activity.title: Try the SSH-only setup
activity.prompt: This is a free switch sandbox, not a graded lab. Type the configuration from this section in order, but first try crypto key generate rsa before setting ip domain-name and read the error. Finish by checking your work with show ip ssh and show running-config.

check.question: Why must a hostname and ip domain-name be configured before crypto key generate rsa?
choices: IOS names the RSA key pair after the device's fully qualified domain name
SSH uses DNS to encrypt each session
The domain name becomes the SSH password
Those commands disable Telnet first
check.explanation: The key is labeled with hostname.domain, so IOS refuses to generate it until both exist ('% Please define a domain-name first'). DNS plays no part in encrypting the session.

sections.title: Verifying and using SSH
sections.body:
After configuring SSH, prove it works and know how to read the evidence.

- **show ip ssh** reports the SSH server: SSH Enabled - version 2.0 once ip ssh version 2 is set. **Version 1.99** means the server accepts both version 1 and version 2 clients, the default before you restrict it. **SSH Disabled** means no RSA key pair exists yet.
- **show ssh** lists the current SSH sessions: connection number, version, encryption and username.
- **show users** lists every line in use, console and vty alike, with the user and idle time, which is how you notice a forgotten session or an unexpected login.
- **show running-config | section line vty** shows the login and transport settings on every vty range in one view.

Cisco devices are SSH clients too. From a router or switch, `ssh -l admin 10.1.99.11` opens a session to another device as user admin, which is how engineers hop from device to device inside a network that only allows management from certain sources.

Defaults differ by platform, so read the configuration rather than assume. The official guide notes that switches typically allow both Telnet and SSH on vty lines by default (transport input all), while many routers default to **transport input none**, which refuses both until you add transport input ssh. If SSH is configured perfectly but the router still refuses every session, check that line.
sections.code:
SW1# show ip ssh
SSH Enabled - version 2.0
Authentication timeout: 120 secs; Authentication retries: 3

SW1# show ssh
Connection Version Mode Encryption  Hmac         State           Username
0          2.0     IN   aes128-cbc  hmac-sha1    Session started admin
0          2.0     OUT  aes128-cbc  hmac-sha1    Session started admin
%No SSHv1 server connections running.

SW1# show users
    Line       User       Host(s)              Idle       Location
*  0 con 0     admin      idle                 00:00:00
   1 vty 0     admin      idle                 00:02:13 10.1.99.50

R1# ssh -l admin 10.1.99.11
Password:
SW1>
sections.pitfall: Assuming a router accepts SSH because SSH is configured. If line vty says transport input none, every session is refused; add transport input ssh.

check.question: show ip ssh on a switch reports SSH Enabled - version 1.99. What does that mean?
choices: Only SSH version 1 is accepted
The server accepts both SSH version 1 and version 2 clients
SSH is disabled until a 1990-bit key is generated
Only SSH version 2 is accepted
check.explanation: Version 1.99 is the compatibility setting that accepts both versions. ip ssh version 2 restricts the server to version 2, after which show ip ssh reports version 2.0.

sections.title: Web management: HTTP and HTTPS
sections.body:
Many devices also offer a web GUI: WLCs always, autonomous APs, small business switches, and IOS routers and switches through a built-in web server. The rule is the same as Telnet versus SSH.

- **HTTP** (TCP port 80): clear text. Credentials and configuration cross the network readable by anyone in the path.
- **HTTPS** (TCP port 443): HTTP inside TLS. The session is encrypted, and the device proves its identity with a certificate (often self-signed on network gear, which is why browsers warn the first time).

On IOS, `ip http server` enables HTTP and `ip http secure-server` enables HTTPS, and `ip http authentication local` makes the web server use local usernames. Best practice is to disable HTTP with `no ip http server` and keep HTTPS only if you actually use the GUI. The same HTTPS service also carries REST APIs and controller-based management, which you will meet in the automation domain.

On Catalyst IOS XE switches and routers the built-in web interface (the WebUI) runs over this same server, and `show ip http server status` shows which of the HTTP and HTTPS servers are enabled. The WLC GUI that you use to create WLANs is reached with HTTPS to the controller's management interface (in-band) or service port (out-of-band), and by default it cannot be reached from wireless clients at all. Autonomous APs and many small business switches also offer HTTP and HTTPS GUIs; the same rule applies: HTTPS only.
sections.code:
SW1(config)# no ip http server
SW1(config)# ip http secure-server
SW1(config)# ip http authentication local
sections.pitfall: Leaving ip http server enabled because 'nobody uses the GUI'. An unused clear-text login page is still an attack surface; turn it off.

check.question: Which option encrypts a web-based management session to a switch?
choices: HTTP on TCP 80
Telnet on TCP 23
HTTP on TCP 8080
HTTPS on TCP 443
check.explanation: HTTPS wraps HTTP in TLS on TCP 443. Plain HTTP on any port, and Telnet, send everything in clear text.

sections.title: AAA with TACACS+ and RADIUS
sections.body:
Local usernames work in a lab, but picture 300 devices and 25 administrators. Someone leaves the company and you must remove their account from 300 configurations. Someone forgets a password: same problem. And local accounts make it hard to see who ran which command.

The answer is **AAA** with a central server such as Cisco ISE:

- **Authentication**: who are you?
- **Authorization**: what are you allowed to do?
- **Accounting**: what did you do (logins, commands)?

The switch becomes an AAA client. An administrator connects with SSH, the switch passes the credentials to the AAA server, and the server answers accept or reject. Two protocols carry that conversation:

- **TACACS+**: developed by Cisco. TCP port **49**. Encrypts the **entire** message body. Keeps authentication, authorization and accounting separate, so it can authorize each command an administrator types and log it. The usual choice for **device administration**.
- **RADIUS**: an open standard. UDP ports **1812** (authentication and authorization) and **1813** (accounting); older servers use 1645 and 1646. Encrypts **only the password**. Combines authentication and authorization in one exchange. The usual choice for **network access**, such as 802.1X on switch ports and Wi-Fi, and VPN users.

The configuration has three parts: `aaa new-model` switches the device to AAA, a server definition gives the server's address and shared secret key, and **method lists** say which methods to try in order. A list named `default` applies automatically to every line (console, AUX and vty) that does not name another list, so a default list changes how you log in at the console too.

Always keep a local fallback. In a method list such as `group tacacs+ local`, the switch tries the next method (local) only when the server **does not respond**. If the server answers and rejects the password, the login fails; it does not fall through to local.
sections.code:
SW1(config)# username admin secret Str0ngPa55
SW1(config)# aaa new-model
SW1(config)# tacacs server ISE1
SW1(config-server-tacacs)# address ipv4 10.1.100.10
SW1(config-server-tacacs)# key T4cacsK3y
SW1(config-server-tacacs)# exit
SW1(config)# aaa authentication login default group tacacs+ local
SW1(config)# aaa authorization exec default group tacacs+ local
SW1(config)# aaa accounting commands 15 default start-stop group tacacs+
sections.pitfall: Entering aaa new-model without a local username and a fallback method. Logins immediately follow the new AAA rules, and you can lock yourself out. Create the local account first and end method lists with local.

check.question: Which protocol encrypts the entire message body and is commonly used for device administration with per-command authorization?
choices: RADIUS
TACACS+
Telnet
SNMPv2c
check.explanation: TACACS+ runs over TCP 49, encrypts the whole payload and separates authorization from authentication, which enables per-command control. RADIUS encrypts only the password and combines authentication and authorization.

sections.title: TACACS+ versus RADIUS in practice
sections.body:
Both protocols carry the same conversation between an AAA client (the switch, router or WLC, also called the network access device) and the AAA server, usually Cisco ISE. The exam wants you to know how they differ and which job each one fits.

- **Transport**: TACACS+ uses TCP port 49, so delivery is reliable and connection-oriented. RADIUS uses UDP 1812 for authentication and authorization and 1813 for accounting (older servers 1645 and 1646).
- **Encryption**: TACACS+ encrypts the whole body of every message. RADIUS hides only the password; usernames and the rest of the attributes travel in clear text.
- **AAA separation**: TACACS+ handles authentication, authorization and accounting as separate exchanges, so the server can authorize each command an administrator types. RADIUS combines authentication and authorization in one reply.
- **Origin**: TACACS+ was developed by Cisco (the exam calls it Cisco proprietary; it was later published as RFC 8907). RADIUS is an open IETF standard (RFC 2865) supported by every vendor.

That leads to the usual split. **Device administration** (who may log in to the network gear, what commands they may run, and an audit trail of what they did) favors **TACACS+**. **Network access** (users and devices joining the network through 802.1X on switch ports and Wi-Fi, VPN logins) uses **RADIUS**, because supplicants, switches and APs everywhere speak it. Many networks run both against the same ISE servers.

The same choice appears on a WLC: an AireOS RADIUS server entry has a Network User check box (authenticate wireless clients) and a Management check box (authenticate administrators logging in to the controller), and TACACS+ servers can be added for administrator logins.
sections.code:
! RADIUS for logins, local account as fallback
SW1(config)# username admin secret Str0ngPa55
SW1(config)# aaa new-model
SW1(config)# radius server ISE1
SW1(config-radius-server)# address ipv4 10.1.100.10 auth-port 1812 acct-port 1813
SW1(config-radius-server)# key R4diusK3y
SW1(config-radius-server)# exit
SW1(config)# aaa authentication login default group radius local

                 TACACS+                       RADIUS
Transport        TCP 49                        UDP 1812/1813 (1645/1646)
Encryption       Entire body                   Password only
AAA functions    Separate                      Authn and authz combined
Origin           Cisco (RFC 8907)              Open standard (RFC 2865)
Typical use      Device administration         Network access (802.1X, VPN)
sections.tip: Memory hook: TACACS+ for the admins at the CLI (TCP, total encryption, per-command control); RADIUS for the users at the port (UDP, password only, everyone supports it).
sections.pitfall: Thinking RADIUS is insecure because it 'does not encrypt'. It does protect the password with the shared secret; what it leaves visible are the username and other attributes.

check.question: Which statement correctly describes RADIUS?
choices: It runs over TCP 49 and encrypts the whole message
It is Cisco proprietary and used mainly for per-command authorization
It runs over UDP, hides only the password and combines authentication with authorization
It cannot be used for 802.1X
check.explanation: RADIUS is an open standard on UDP 1812 and 1813 that encrypts only the password field and returns authentication and authorization together. TCP 49, full encryption and per-command authorization describe TACACS+. RADIUS is the protocol 802.1X relies on.

sections.title: Cloud-managed devices
sections.body:
A company has 80 small branches and no network staff at any of them. With **cloud-managed** devices, such as the Cisco Meraki line of APs, switches and security appliances, the management plane lives in the vendor's cloud instead of on premises. It works like this:

- The devices are claimed into the organization's account in the cloud dashboard, by serial number or order number.
- At the branch, someone plugs a device in. It gets an address, connects outbound over the internet to the cloud, and downloads its configuration and firmware. This is zero-touch provisioning.
- Administrators configure, monitor and troubleshoot every site from one web dashboard. The cloud also collects statistics, raises alerts and schedules firmware updates.

Only management and monitoring traffic goes to the cloud. User traffic is forwarded locally by the devices. If a branch loses its connection to the cloud, its network keeps forwarding with the last configuration; you just cannot change it or see live statistics until the connection returns.

Compare the three ways to manage devices. **Device by device**: console, SSH and HTTPS to each box. **Controller-based**: an on-premises controller you run yourself, such as a WLC or Cisco Catalyst Center (formerly DNA Center). **Cloud-managed**: the controller role becomes a subscription service. The trade-offs: fast multi-site rollout and no controller hardware to maintain, against depending on internet access for management and paying an ongoing license. The same idea is spreading beyond Meraki-branded gear: Cisco now lets many Catalyst switches and APs be managed or monitored from the Meraki dashboard, and the exam simply asks you to recognize the model, not a product list.
sections.code:
Meraki cloud dashboard
                       ^
     management only   |   (each device connects outbound over HTTPS/TLS)
            +----------+----------+
            |                     |
       Branch 1 AP          Branch 2 switch
            |                     |
   user traffic stays local at each branch
sections.pitfall: Assuming a cloud outage takes the branch offline. Forwarding continues locally; only configuration changes and monitoring wait for the cloud.

check.question: In a Meraki cloud-managed network, what happens to user traffic if a branch loses its connection to the cloud dashboard?
choices: It stops until the dashboard is reachable again
It is redirected through the nearest WLC
It keeps flowing locally using the last configuration
It is dropped except for DNS
check.explanation: The cloud holds the management plane only. Devices keep forwarding traffic with their last configuration; changes and live monitoring resume when the cloud connection returns.

sections.title: Choosing and locking down management access
sections.body:
Every management method has a place, and every insecure one has a secure replacement. The table pulls the ports and properties together; know it cold for the exam. Restricting sources is the other half of hardening: a standard ACL applied to the vty lines with `access-class 10 in` lets only the management subnet open Telnet or SSH sessions, whatever their credentials.

A hardening checklist that ties this lesson to the security domain later in the path:

- Use SSH version 2 only (`transport input ssh`) on every vty line, and disable Telnet.
- Use HTTPS only (`no ip http server`), or disable the web server entirely if nobody uses it.
- Authenticate administrators through AAA (TACACS+ for device administration) and keep a local fallback account.
- Restrict which addresses can reach the vty lines with an ACL applied by `access-class` under line vty.
- Set `exec-timeout` so idle sessions close.
- Keep console access available out-of-band for emergencies, protected with login local.
- Put management interfaces in a dedicated management VLAN or an out-of-band network.
sections.code:
Method     Port          Encrypted?          Typical use
Console    serial        n/a (physical)      Initial setup, recovery, outages
Telnet     TCP 23        No                  Avoid; legacy only
SSH        TCP 22        Yes                 Remote CLI
HTTP       TCP 80        No                  Avoid; disable it
HTTPS      TCP 443       Yes (TLS)           Web GUI, REST APIs
TACACS+    TCP 49        Whole body          AAA for device administration
RADIUS     UDP 1812/1813 Password only       AAA for network access (802.1X, VPN)
Cloud      HTTPS out     Yes                 Meraki dashboard management

! Only the management subnet may reach the vty lines
SW1(config)# access-list 10 permit 10.1.99.0 0.0.0.255
SW1(config)# line vty 0 15
SW1(config-line)# access-class 10 in
sections.pitfall: Hardening the vty lines but leaving the HTTP server on. Attackers try every management door, so close all the ones you do not use.

check.question: An audit finds that a router accepts management logins over TCP 23 and TCP 80. Which changes fix both findings?
choices: ip ssh version 1 and ip http secure-server
no cdp run and no lldp run
transport input ssh on all vty lines and no ip http server
exec-timeout 0 0 and ip http server
check.explanation: TCP 23 is Telnet, closed by allowing only SSH on the vty lines, and TCP 80 is the HTTP server, closed with no ip http server. exec-timeout 0 0 would actually disable the idle timeout.

keyTerms.definition: Serial management port (9600 baud, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit) used with a rollover or USB cable.
Management access that does not depend on the production network, such as the console or a separate management network.
Management over the production network to a device's IP address: Telnet, SSH, HTTP, HTTPS, SNMP.
A virtual terminal line that accepts one remote Telnet or SSH session; configured under line vty.
Secure Shell, TCP 22: encrypted remote CLI. Needs a hostname, domain name, RSA keys and username login.
TCP 23 remote CLI that sends everything, including passwords, in clear text.
HTTP over TLS on TCP 443: encrypted web management, enabled on IOS with ip http secure-server.
Authentication, authorization and accounting, usually provided by a central server such as Cisco ISE.
Cisco-developed AAA protocol on TCP 49 that encrypts the whole body and separates the three A's; used for device administration.
Open-standard AAA protocol on UDP 1812/1813 that encrypts only the password; used for network access such as 802.1X.
Devices (such as Meraki) configured and monitored from a vendor cloud dashboard while forwarding user traffic locally.
Asynchronous serial port on older routers for out-of-band access through a dial-in modem.
Global command that sets the privileged EXEC password as a hash; overrides enable password.
Line command that authenticates users against the local username database.
vty line command choosing which protocols may connect: ssh, telnet, all or none.
Line command that applies an ACL to vty lines to limit which source addresses can log in.
An ordered list of AAA methods (for example group tacacs+ then local); the default list applies to every line without a named list.

summary: The console (9600 8N1), AUX port and dedicated management ports give out-of-band access; Telnet, SSH, HTTP and HTTPS are in-band.
Lines authenticate with a shared password (login), local usernames (login local) or AAA; use enable secret, never enable password.
A Layer 2 switch is managed through an SVI address plus ip default-gateway; remote sessions use vty lines.
SSH-only access: hostname, ip domain-name, crypto key generate rsa, ip ssh version 2, local username, login local and transport input ssh on all vty lines; verify with show ip ssh and show ssh.
Use HTTPS (443) instead of HTTP (80); disable unused web servers with no ip http server.
TACACS+ (TCP 49, full encryption, separate AAA) suits device administration; RADIUS (UDP 1812/1813, password only) suits network access such as 802.1X.
Cloud-managed devices get configuration from the vendor cloud; user traffic stays local and keeps flowing if the cloud is unreachable.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a new network technician the different ways to get into a switch, from the console cable to SSH and the web GUI, why Telnet and HTTP are unsafe, and how a TACACS+ server makes managing 300 devices easier than local usernames.

questions.question: Which terminal emulator settings are the defaults for a Cisco console port?
choices: 115200 bps, 8 data bits, even parity, 2 stop bits
9600 bps, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit
9600 bps, 7 data bits, odd parity, 1 stop bit
19200 bps, 8 data bits, no parity, 2 stop bits
questions.explanation: Cisco console ports default to 9600 bps, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit and no flow control, often written 9600 8N1.

questions.question: Which is an example of out-of-band management?
choices: SSH to the switch's management SVI
HTTPS to the WLC's management interface
A console server cabled to device console ports over a separate network
SNMP polling across the production network
questions.explanation: Out-of-band access does not rely on the production network. A console server reaches each device's console port independently, so it still works when the data network is down.

questions.question: Which TCP port does SSH use?
questions.explanation: SSH listens on TCP 22. Telnet uses TCP 23.

questions.question: Which TCP port does Telnet use?
questions.explanation: Telnet uses TCP 23 and sends everything, including passwords, in clear text.

questions.question: Match each management protocol to its port.
questions.explanation: Note the transport split for AAA: TACACS+ uses TCP, RADIUS uses UDP (1812 for authentication, 1813 for accounting).

questions.question: Type the global command that sets a Layer 2 switch's default gateway to 10.1.99.1.
questions.explanation: A Layer 2 switch does not route, so ip default-gateway tells it where to send replies to hosts outside its management subnet.

questions.question: Where is the management IP address configured on a Layer 2 switch?
choices: On the physical uplink port
Under line vty 0 15
On the console line
On an SVI such as interface vlan 99
questions.explanation: Switchports carry no IP address, so the switch's own address goes on a switch virtual interface in the management VLAN.

questions.question: Put the steps of a TACACS+ login to a switch in order.
items: The administrator opens an SSH session to the switch
The switch prompts for a username and password
The switch sends the credentials to the TACACS+ server
The server replies with accept or reject
The switch grants or denies access to the CLI
questions.explanation: The switch is only the AAA client: it collects the credentials, the server decides, and the switch enforces the answer.

questions.question: In line configuration mode for the vty lines, type the command that allows only SSH for remote logins.
questions.explanation: transport input ssh refuses Telnet on those lines. Apply it to every vty line the device has.

questions.question: Type the global command that generates a 2048-bit RSA key pair for SSH without prompting for the size.
accept: crypto key generate rsa general-keys modulus 2048
questions.explanation: Adding modulus 2048 avoids the size prompt. SSH version 2 needs at least 768 bits, and 2048 is the usual choice.

questions.question: The engineer is trying to enable SSH. What must be configured before this command will succeed?
questions.code:
Switch(config)# hostname SW1
SW1(config)# crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048
% Please define a domain-name first.
choices: ip ssh version 2
ip domain-name example.com
username admin secret Str0ngPa55
transport input ssh
questions.explanation: The key is named after hostname.domain, so a domain name is required (the hostname is already set). The other commands are part of the SSH setup but do not affect key generation.

questions.question: A security scan shows this switch still accepts Telnet, even though SSH is configured. Based on the configuration, why?
questions.code:
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input ssh
line vty 5 15
 login local
 transport input telnet ssh
choices: ip ssh version 2 always allows Telnet as a fallback
login local permits Telnet on every line
Lines 5 to 15 still allow Telnet
The RSA key is shorter than 2048 bits
questions.explanation: Each group of vty lines has its own transport setting. Lines 5 to 15 accept telnet and ssh, so a Telnet session lands on one of them. Set transport input ssh on line vty 0 15.

questions.question: show ip ssh on a switch returns 'SSH Disabled - version 1.99' and asks you to create RSA keys. What is the most likely reason SSH is disabled?
choices: No RSA key pair has been generated
transport input ssh is missing
The domain name is too long
Telnet is still enabled on the vty lines
questions.explanation: The SSH server runs only once an RSA key pair exists. Without keys, show ip ssh reports SSH disabled regardless of the vty settings.

questions.question: Which three are required for a switch to accept SSH logins that use local usernames? (Choose three.)
choices: An RSA key pair
A local username with a password or secret
login local on the vty lines
ip http secure-server
An SNMP community string
questions.explanation: SSH needs keys (which in turn need a hostname and domain name), a username to authenticate, and vty lines that check the local database. HTTPS and SNMP are unrelated.

questions.question: Type the global command that disables the clear-text HTTP server on IOS.
questions.explanation: no ip http server stops the TCP 80 web server. ip http secure-server controls the HTTPS server separately.

questions.question: Why is HTTPS preferred over HTTP for managing a device through its web GUI?
choices: HTTPS loads pages faster
HTTP cannot display configuration pages
HTTPS encrypts the session with TLS, protecting credentials and configuration
HTTPS does not require a username
questions.explanation: HTTP sends logins and configuration in clear text. HTTPS encrypts the session and lets the device prove its identity with a certificate.

questions.question: Match each part of AAA to the question it answers.

pairs.right: What are you allowed to do?

questions.explanation: Authentication proves identity, authorization grants privileges, and accounting records activity such as logins and commands.

questions.question: Which statement correctly compares TACACS+ and RADIUS?
choices: TACACS+ uses UDP 1812, and RADIUS uses TCP 49
Both encrypt only the password
RADIUS separates authentication and authorization, while TACACS+ combines them
TACACS+ uses TCP 49 and encrypts the whole body; RADIUS uses UDP and encrypts only the password
questions.explanation: TACACS+ runs on TCP 49, encrypts the full payload and separates the AAA functions. RADIUS runs on UDP 1812/1813, encrypts just the password and combines authentication with authorization.

questions.question: Which two statements describe RADIUS? (Choose two.)
choices: It is an open standard
It uses TCP port 49
It combines authentication and authorization
It encrypts the entire message body
It is Cisco proprietary
questions.explanation: RADIUS is an open standard over UDP that combines authentication and authorization and encrypts only the password. TCP 49, full encryption and Cisco origin describe TACACS+.

questions.question: A switch uses aaa authentication login default group tacacs+ local. The TACACS+ server is reachable and rejects user bob's password. What happens?
choices: The login fails; local is tried only when the server does not respond
The switch checks bob's password against the local database
The switch admits bob with read-only access
The switch keeps retrying the server until it accepts
questions.explanation: A method list moves to the next method only on an error, such as no response from the server. A reject is a final answer, so the local fallback is not used.

questions.question: Which AAA protocol would you normally use to authenticate wireless users with 802.1X?
choices: TACACS+
RADIUS
SSH
LDAP over Telnet
questions.explanation: RADIUS is the standard protocol for network access control, including 802.1X on Wi-Fi and wired ports. TACACS+ is typically used for administrators logging in to network devices.

questions.question: Type the global command that enables the AAA model on IOS.
questions.explanation: aaa new-model activates AAA so that aaa authentication, authorization and accounting commands take effect. Create a local fallback user first so you cannot lock yourself out.

questions.question: How does a new Meraki device get its configuration when it is first plugged in at a branch?
choices: An engineer must connect to the console and paste the configuration
It connects outbound to the Meraki cloud and downloads the configuration assigned to it in the dashboard
It receives it from a local WLC over CAPWAP
It copies the configuration of its CDP neighbor
questions.explanation: Cloud-managed devices are claimed in the dashboard ahead of time. When powered on with internet access, they contact the cloud and download their configuration and firmware: zero-touch provisioning.

questions.question: Which statement about cloud-managed networks is true?
choices: All user traffic is tunneled through the vendor's cloud
Each device must be configured locally before the cloud can see it
Management and monitoring happen in the cloud, while user traffic is forwarded locally
Cloud management requires an on-premises controller at every site
questions.explanation: The cloud hosts the management plane only. Devices forward user data locally, and no on-site controller is needed.

questions.question: Which cable traditionally connects a PC's serial port to a Cisco RJ-45 console port?
choices: Crossover cable
Straight-through cable
Fiber patch cable
Rollover (console) cable
questions.explanation: The console cable is a rollover cable, usually with a USB-to-serial adapter on modern laptops. Many newer devices also offer a USB console port.

questions.question: In line configuration mode, type the command that disconnects sessions after 10 minutes of inactivity.
questions.explanation: exec-timeout takes minutes and seconds. exec-timeout 0 0 disables the timeout, which is a bad idea on production lines.

questions.question: Why do networks use a TACACS+ or RADIUS server instead of local usernames on every device?
questions.answer: A central AAA server keeps one database of administrators, so accounts are added, changed or removed in one place, and it can authorize commands and log who did what. Local usernames must be maintained on every device separately.
questions.explanation: Centralized AAA scales to hundreds of devices and gives accountability; a local account remains only as an emergency fallback.

questions.question: A switch is configured with line vty 0 15. How many simultaneous Telnet or SSH sessions can it accept? (Number only.)
questions.explanation: Lines 0 through 15 are 16 vty lines, and each remote session uses one.

questions.question: Policy: administrators must use an encrypted CLI, and only from the management subnet 10.1.99.0/24. Which configuration meets both requirements?
choices: transport input ssh plus an access-class ACL permitting 10.1.99.0/24 on all vty lines
transport input telnet plus ip http secure-server
no ip http server plus exec-timeout 0 0
login local on the console plus ip ssh version 1
questions.explanation: transport input ssh enforces encryption, and access-class applies an ACL to the vty lines so only the management subnet can connect. The other options leave Telnet or SSH v1 in use or do not restrict sources.

questions.question: Based on this configuration, what happens when an administrator opens a Telnet session to the switch?
questions.code:
username admin secret Str0ngPa55
!
line vty 0 15
 password Cisco123
 login local
 transport input telnet ssh
choices: It asks only for the line password Cisco123
It asks for a username and password and accepts admin with Str0ngPa55
It refuses the session because both password and login local are set
It allows the session with no authentication
questions.explanation: line vty uses login local, so the switch prompts for a username and password from the local database (admin with Str0ngPa55). The line password Cisco123 is ignored with login local, and Telnet is allowed because transport input includes it.

questions.question: Type the global command that sets the privileged EXEC password to Ccna2026 and stores it as a hash.
questions.explanation: enable secret stores a hashed password and overrides any enable password. enable password stores it in clear text and should not be used.

questions.question: A new switch has an IP address, and its vty lines show only the default login command. An engineer telnets to it. What happens?
choices: The session opens straight into user EXEC mode
The session opens straight into privileged EXEC mode
The switch refuses the session: password required, but none set
The switch asks for a username from the local database
questions.explanation: With login but no password configured, the switch refuses every vty session with "Password required, but none set". Configure a password, login local with a user, or AAA first.

questions.question: Based on this output, which change makes the switch refuse SSH version 1 clients?
questions.code:
SW1# show ip ssh
SSH Enabled - version 1.99
Authentication timeout: 120 secs; Authentication retries: 3
choices: transport input ssh under line vty 0 15
crypto key generate rsa modulus 4096
no ip http server
ip ssh version 2
questions.explanation: Version 1.99 means the server accepts both SSH versions. ip ssh version 2 restricts it to version 2. Regenerating keys or changing transport input does not change the protocol version accepted.

questions.question: From R1's privileged EXEC prompt, type the command that opens an SSH session to 10.1.99.11 as user admin.
questions.explanation: Cisco IOS includes an SSH client: ssh -l username address. It lets you hop between devices from inside the network.

questions.question: A new router has a local user, an RSA key and ip ssh version 2, but both SSH and Telnet sessions are refused. Its configuration shows this. What is the fix?
questions.code:
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input none
choices: Add transport input ssh under line vty 0 4
Remove login local
Generate the RSA key again with a larger modulus
Add ip http secure-server
questions.explanation: transport input none refuses every protocol on those lines, a common router default. transport input ssh allows SSH only, which is what the policy wants. Generating keys again does not change the line settings.

questions.question: Match each line configuration to how users authenticate.

pairs.right: One shared line password, no username
Usernames and secrets stored on the device

pairs.left: aaa authentication login default group tacacs+ local
pairs.right: AAA server first, local accounts if it does not respond

questions.explanation: login uses the line password, login local uses usernames on the device, AAA method lists send credentials to a server (with fallbacks), and a console with no login lets anyone in.

questions.question: An admin in 10.2.0.0/16 must manage a Layer 2 switch whose management address is in 10.1.99.0/24 using SSH with local accounts. Which four are required on the switch? (Choose four.)
choices: An IP address on an up SVI in the management VLAN
ip default-gateway pointing to the management subnet's router
ip routing
An RSA key pair
login local on the vty lines with a local username
ip http secure-server
questions.explanation: The switch needs an up SVI with its address, a default gateway to reply off-subnet, an RSA key (which needs a hostname and domain name) and vty lines that authenticate usernames. A Layer 2 switch does not need ip routing, and the HTTPS server is unrelated to SSH.

questions.question: Type the global command that makes the default login method list try RADIUS servers first and the local database if no RADIUS server responds.
questions.answer: aaa authentication login default group radius local
questions.explanation: aaa authentication login default group radius local applies to every line that does not name another list. local is used only when no RADIUS server answers, not when one rejects the user.

questions.question: After aaa new-model and aaa authentication login default group tacacs+ local, the console suddenly asks for a username, and only TACACS+ accounts work there. Why?
choices: aaa new-model disables the console port
The default method list applies to all lines, the console included, unless a named list is applied there
TACACS+ servers always take over the console
The console needs exec-timeout 0 0 to bypass AAA
questions.explanation: A method list named default applies to every line that does not reference a named list, including the console. To treat the console differently, create a named list (for example local only) and apply it with login authentication NAME under line console 0.

questions.question: Which management model uses an on-premises controller that the organization runs itself, such as a WLC or Cisco Catalyst Center?
choices: Controller-based management
Cloud-managed
Device-by-device management
Out-of-band console management
questions.explanation: Controller-based management keeps the controller on site. Cloud-managed moves that role to the vendor's cloud (Meraki), and device-by-device management uses console, SSH and HTTPS to each box.

questions.question: On an AireOS WLC, a RADIUS server entry must authenticate administrators who log in to the controller GUI, not wireless clients. Which option enables that?
choices: Network User
Server Status Disabled
Management
Mgmt Via Wireless
questions.explanation: Each RADIUS server entry has a Network User check box (authenticate wireless clients) and a Management check box (authenticate administrators logging in to the WLC). Tick Management for admin logins.
